title: Asteroid 1999 AN10, 1.8 km Across, to Pass as Close as Lunar Orbit in August 2027; NASA Tracking

content:
Near-Earth asteroid 1999 AN10 will make a close approach on August 7, 2027, coming within about 389,855 km of Earth—roughly comparable to the average distance between Earth and the Moon. Its estimated diameter is between 800 meters and 1.8 km. NASA classifies it as a "potentially hazardous asteroid (PHA)," but there is said to be no impact risk at closest approach. The passage of such a large body at this proximity is also valuable from an observational standpoint, and it may be visible with binoculars.

Closest approach will occur at 7:12 a.m. Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), or around 4:12 p.m. Japan time. The geocentric distance will be about 389,855 km, nearly the same as the average distance between Earth and the Moon. Its distance from the Moon will be about 763,391 km, roughly twice its distance from Earth. It will not enter the atmosphere and will simply continue along its orbit.

The "potentially hazardous" designation does not mean an imminent collision. Under NASA's definition, it applies to small bodies with a diameter of 140 meters or more whose orbits could bring them within 0.05 astronomical units (one astronomical unit is the average distance between the Sun and Earth, about 150 million km) of Earth's orbital path. 1999 AN10 was designated because it meets the size and orbital criteria, and current orbital calculations show neither a 2027 collision nor any impact on the Moon.

1999 AN10 was discovered on January 13, 1999, by astronomers at the Lincoln Laboratory Experimental Test Site (ETS) in New Mexico. It belongs to the Apollo group, which crosses Earth's orbit, and travels around the Sun on an elongated orbit extending beyond Mars' orbit with a period of 643 days.

Observationally, its apparent brightness at closest approach is projected to reach about magnitude 7.3. While difficult to see with the naked eye, it may be visible with binoculars. Unlike stars, asteroids move significantly against the background star field. According to the astronomy information site EarthSky, on the night of August 7, 2027, it will pass through the regions of Taurus, Aries, Pisces, and Pegasus.

This close approach is also important for improving the precision of orbital calculations. When first discovered, the asteroid was thought to pose a possible collision risk with Earth in 2044 or 2046. Accumulating position data at closest approach will improve prediction accuracy and contribute to formulating strategies for planetary defense—protecting Earth from celestial impacts.

Demonstrations of planetary defense technology are already underway. NASA's DART probe, launched in late 2021, struck the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. When it hit at about 6 km per second (more than 13,000 mph), Dimorphos' orbital period was shortened by 33 minutes—far exceeding the original goal of one minute or more. In addition to the recoil from the impact itself, the effect of ejected debris pushing the asteroid is believed to have been significant.

The European Space Agency (ESA) launched the Hera probe in October 2024, sending it toward Didymos and Dimorphos. After a Mars flyby, it entered its arrival phase and successfully captured its first images from a distance of about 800 miles (about 1,300 km). In early November, detailed images of Didymos were also released. Hera is the first mission to closely explore a binary asteroid system, examining the traces of the DART impact and Dimorphos' mass. Determining the mass is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of planetary defense technology. In January 2027, it plans to release the small satellites Juventas and Milani to attempt surface landings and radar exploration down to 100 meters below the surface.

Understanding of near-Earth asteroids has advanced rapidly over the past quarter-century. In 2000, about 300 near-Earth asteroids had been confirmed; today the number exceeds 43,000. With the expansion of observation networks, the discovery of hazardous candidates and the precision of orbital tracking are steadily improving.

The next focus is Apophis, which will approach Earth on April 13, 2029. The roughly 340-meter body will pass at an extraordinary close range of about 31,200 km above the surface. That is inside the geostationary orbit where weather and broadcasting satellites circle, but there is no risk of collision. It is expected to be visible to the naked eye across wide areas of Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia, as well as parts of South America, and ESA's RAMSES project and NASA's OSIRIS-APEX mission plan to investigate it with spacecraft.

These observations will accumulate data on both the orbital prediction of small bodies and defense technology. Although 1999 AN10's 2027 approach is not an impact crisis, it is positioned as a valuable opportunity for researchers to precisely determine the orbit of a large body.
